item.title: For students with their sights set on space medicine, a new community takes flight
item.description: MIT’s Doctors Without Gravity club connects health and space science enthusiasts.

item.title: Using eyedrops in space—wearable patch offers a new approach
item.description: Applying eyedrops is difficult in space, where there is almost no gravity. A KAIST research team has developed a wearable patch that delivers eyedrops to the eye without relying on gravity. The research team was led by Professor Ki-Hun Jeong from the Department of Bio and Brain Engineering, in collaboration with a research team led by Professor Se Joon Woo from Seoul National University Bundang Hospital. The paper is published in the journal Sensors and Actuators B: Chemical.

item.title: Aurora supercomputer powers two of the largest cosmological simulations to date
item.description: Researchers at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Argonne National Laboratory have completed two of the largest cosmological simulations ever performed. Each simulation modeled the evolution of 13.4 trillion dark matter particles across a region 28.6 billion light-years wide.

item.title: Planetary 'twins' Uranus and Neptune may have different origin stories
item.description: By indirectly probing the depths of Uranus and Neptune's atmospheres, an international team of scientists has revealed a significant contrast in their chemical composition. Neptune appears to be more enriched in oxygen than Uranus. These results suggest that the two ice giants may have formed in different regions of the primitive solar system before reaching their current orbits, calling into question the idea of a common origin for these two planets, often considered twins.

item.title: Cosmic 'hamburger' offers rare edge-on view of where giant planets may take shape
item.description: Astronomers using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) were surprised to discover the earliest phases of giant planet formation between the dense layers of gas and dust in the "Gomez's Hamburger" system, referred to as GoHam.

item.title: NASA's CASALS instrument bridges gaps in 3D maps of Earth's surface
item.description: A team of researchers at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) has developed a new instrument designed to eliminate blind spots between lines of lidar data on Earth's surface. Built with support from NASA's Earth Science Technology Office (ESTO), the Concurrent Artificially-intelligent Spectrometry Lidar System (CASALS) could help researchers map the features of Earth's surface in detail. item.title: Reexamined Viking 2 signal reveals possible marsquake from region active decades later
item.description: Earthquakes and the seismic waves they generate provide some of the best clues to Earth's interior. To extend that success to other worlds, scientists placed seismometers on the Apollo missions to the moon and on the Viking Mars landers, which reached Mars in 1976. Though the Apollo detectors proved a resounding success, Viking's results on Mars were less clear: Viking 1's seismometer failed to deploy properly, and Viking 2 recorded only two ambiguous events.

item.title: There Should Be Black Holes in our Neighbourhood. Can We Find Them?
item.description: Stellar-mass black holes should be in our neighbourhood within about 50 light years of the Solar System. But they're likely isolated, without much to feed on, making them difficult to find. Gaia found some candidates, but confirming them is tough.

item.title: A Stubborn Question Answered: New Research Reveals How the Milky Way's Disk Formed
item.description: Figuring out how the Milky Way's thin and thick disks formed is a tough question in astronomy. It relies on determining individual stellar ages accurately. Gaia was pretty good at that, and new research based on its data may have found the answer.

item.title: Neutrinos May Be The Key To Why We Are Surrounded By Matter
item.description: In the early Universe, neutrinos interacted strongly with other matter before some of them "decoupled." The heaviest of these decoupled neutrinos may be the solution to the matter-antimatter cosmic mystery.

item.title: Under Extreme Pressure on Ice Giants, Water Ice Gets Weird
item.description: On Earth, water ice is simply water ice. But under extreme pressure, it takes on an unusual asymmetric form. It stops being molecular and its atoms are forced into a strange asymmetry.

item.title: SpaceX turns a profit after a string of losses as its satellite and computer leasing businesses soar
item.description: SpaceX reported a bigger quarterly profit than expected Tuesday as its satellite communications operations and its business of leasing computing power to other companies boomed.

item.title: The Orionid meteor shower is coming. Here's how and when to watch
item.description: The Orionids—one of two major meteor showers caused by remnants from Halley's Comet—will peak this week, though a large moon will dim visibility until after it sets late at night.

item.title: The Gas Near Sagittarius A-star is Enriched in Metals, Probably from Supernovae Explosions
item.description: The region near Sagittarius A-star, the Milky Way's supermassive black hole, is enriched in metals, although only modestly. The likely cause is supernovae explosions, which synthesize elements heavier than hydrogen and helium. Over time, this metal-rich gas found its way towards the SMBH. The increased metallicity and heat from the supernova affect how fast gas flows into the SMBH.

item.title: Understanding celestial coordinates
item.description: Just as we use latitude and longitude to know the precise position of something on Earth’s surface, it’s useful to have a system for knowing the position of objects in the heavens. item.title: Lucy mission marks 5 years of discoveries
item.description: On Oct. 16, 2021, NASA's Lucy spacecraft began its journey to the never-before-explored Jupiter Trojan asteroids with an early morning launch. Now less than a year away from the first-ever close-up of a Trojan, the Southwest Research Institute–led mission has already made several findings during its first five years.

item.title: JWST Tracks Shifting Water Clouds and Churning Gases on the Coldest Known Brown Dwarf
item.description: When picturing a star, typically people think of giant balls of burning gas in the sky that emit enough light they are hard to miss. Planets, on the other hand, come in one of two general categories - rocky worlds like Earth or gas giants similar to Jupiter. But there is a third category of astronomical object that doesn’t really fit either of those descriptions, and also doesn’t exist in our own solar system. item.title: Near miss: Indonesia probes crash of suspected Chinese rocket fragment
item.description: Indonesian authorities were investigating Tuesday after a car-sized piece of debris, possibly from a Chinese rocket according to a government agency, crashed into a palm oil plantation near homes and work sites.

item.title: Achievement Unlocked: Microblazar Confirmed
item.description: Researchers have confirmed the existence of the first microblazar. Unlike blazars, which are extragalctic and powered by supermassive black holes, microblazars are inside the Milky Way, and are powered by stellar mass black holes. The microblazar may be the source for the most energetic particles in the galaxy.

item.title: Why the Drake equation is still important 65 years after its creation
item.description: The Drake equation provides a way to guess how many aliens we might be able to communicate with, but it’s also a prime example of the importance of scientific guessing, says columnist Leah Crane

item.title: A lack of rockets is creating a crisis for space technology companies
item.description: SpaceX’s changing priorities, the war in Ukraine and a lack of competitors are all causing a launch crisis that might last years

item.title: Margaret Hamilton, computing pioneer who led software development for the Apollo program, dies at 90
item.description: Over two decades at MIT, Hamilton forged new paths in computer science and engineering. Her groundbreaking work included leading the team that programmed the first computers that took humans to the moon.

item.title: SpaceX’s Starship will orbit Earth for first time during next flight
item.description: Starship's next test flight will be its first orbital mission. The craft will also release working Starlink V3 satellites for the first time, making the flight the first commercially useful Starship mission
